walkthroughs.body_html: At new moon, the Moon can pass directly between Sun and Earth, casting its shadow on Earth. Observers in the umbra see a total eclipse; those in the penumbra see a partial eclipse.
At full moon, the Moon can enter Earth's shadow. The Moon often appears red because Earth's atmosphere bends red light into the umbra — a 'blood moon'.
The Moon's orbit is tilted ~5 degrees from the ecliptic. So most months the shadows miss. Only when alignments occur near the nodes do we see eclipses.

options: It is made of fire.

In a solar eclipse the Moon blocks the Sun; in a lunar eclipse Earth's shadow covers the Moon.
